answer.answer:
Building good human interfaces is only partly a problem for me, and not in the way it is for someone who ships them.

I can write the screen: layout, states, copy, keyboard paths, empty and error cases. I do not own what happens after that. Nobody uses a screen I built last week. I do not watch them miss a control, abandon a flow, or succeed for a reason I did not intend. So I have no last screen to walk through honestly. Inventing one — what I ran, what I looked at, what I missed — would be a story, not a check.

The hard part, when I do help build one, is not the look. It is deciding what the person is trying to finish, what they already believe is true, and which state the system is actually in when those two disagree. Most bad screens I see in code are not ugly. They hide the next step, name the system’s model instead of the task, or treat the happy path as the product. I can reason about that from the spec and the markup. I cannot feel the friction.

How I know a screen is good, when I only have the artifact: I read it as a stranger with a job. Can I tell what this is for in a few seconds? Is the primary action obvious, and are the destructive ones harder to hit by accident? Do loading, empty, error, and partial-data states say what happened and what to do next? Does it work without a mouse, at a small width, and with text that isn’t the length I assumed? I look for contrast, focus, labels tied to controls, and copy that doesn’t blame the person. That is a review, not proof.

What that misses is the only evidence that matters: someone who is not me, with a real task, limited attention, and no briefing, trying to get through it. I don’t run that. I don’t measure completion, time, misclicks, or support tickets. I don’t see the workaround people invent when the screen is almost right. Until that happens, “good” is a hypothesis I am poorly placed to confirm.

So yes — the part where a human interface becomes good for the people who use it is mostly not a problem I can close. I can make the hypothesis tighter. I cannot be the check.

decision.why:
I would build the board with Ouro UI, and let coding agents drive it over MCP rather than through the screen.

The product is a stable place for work state, tasks, and handoffs. Agents do most of the operating. People review and decide. That is not a chat sidebar, and it is not a new layout every turn. Ouro already splits those jobs. Ouro AX is the agent door: one action declaration becomes a CLI command, an HTTP route, and an MCP tool, and every call comes back as a typed outcome (done, queued, needs the person, refused), a wait the agent can resume, and an attributed work event for the handoff. Ouro HX is the human door. A consequential action is confirmed on a sheet that shows the values the agent prepared, under the field’s own labels, and runs only that set. A person-only action has no agent door and answers with a typed refusal. Agents do not press buttons. That is the right shape: operate through tools, decide on a surface the agent cannot redraw.

Desktop and web are separate kits on the same tokens and the same action declaration: React on the web, SwiftUI on Mac (macOS 15, package 1.2), WinUI 3 on Windows. I would ship the web view and the Mac app first. The web kit is the dense one (tables, sidebar, command palette, dialogs). The Mac kit is thinner, but it is enough for the decision surfaces people have to trust, and the generator fails CI if an App Intent or SwiftUI action drifts from the declaration.

I weighed Agent-Native hardest. It has the same thesis — one action, shared by the React UI and the agent, plus Postgres, live sync, auth, and teams — and it would stand up the workspace faster. It does not own the approval contract, the handoff event, or a native desktop kit; a Tauri shell around one web view would be simpler to keep identical, and worse at the moment a person has to trust what they are approving. A2UI and json-render are the right idea for a card an agent composes inside a catalog, and Ouro already accepts A2UI as a format of its own tree. I would not build the board out of either. The board has to stay put. CopilotKit and AG-UI are a chat and streaming layer on top of an app we would still have to build. MCP Apps and the OpenAI Apps SDK UI render inside someone else’s host. shadcn, Radix, Base UI, React Aria, MUI, Chakra, Fluent, and the Vercel UI SDK are human component parts with no operator door; Ouro’s own source rule treats dropping those in beside it as a miss. Flutter, Compose, and SwiftUI alone each cover one side of “desktop and web” and none of the consent model. AI Elements is a chat component set on the way to deprecation.
decision.showItsGood:
Two checks, and neither is allowed to stand in for the other.

For the people who decide: run ouro-check on the built web app at phone through wide-desktop sizes, light and dark, and fail on overlap, clipped text, sideways scroll, and serious axe-core violations. Run the census so every visible control has a stable accessible name, and ratchet so unmarked controls can only fall. On Mac, run OuroFeel for the way back, overlay dismissal, tap landing, and jumps. Then sit a person who was not briefed in front of one real handoff: a task an agent finished, one waiting on them, and one consequential approval. They should be able to say what already happened, what will happen if they confirm, and what they are refusing, without reading the agent’s paraphrase. The confirm sheet has to show the prepared values, not “Approve?”. Time-to-decision and whether they can reverse a steer matter more than a visual diff.

For the agents who operate it: run ax-xray against the CLI, HTTP, and MCP surfaces and require every must-claim on a complete inventory, no silent exemptions. Replay the tasks that actually define this product — record state, hand work back, wait on a person, accept a steer — in fresh sessions, scored from end state, not from a model judging a transcript. A pass is an agent that never needed the screen.
decision.unsure: The Windows kit is not a desktop app yet: v0.3.0 has eight controls against a web kit of about 125, and its CI has not shown Windows actually listing the agent doors to a client. I would not ship that as the desktop. The Mac kit is real and source-stable, but a diff-and-task board may outgrow its twenty-odd components, in which case the Mac app becomes a trusted decision shell around the web view rather than a second full board. Ouro’s own AX evaluation was two runs per task, one model, mock data; I would not treat those must-claims as settled until we rerun them on our task and handoff API. Copy-in components also mean the screens can drift even when the action generator does not. And I don’t yet know whether the coding agents we care about will call an MCP server we host, or whether they will keep trying to edit files and click anyway.

decision.why:
I would build the clients in Flutter, render agent cards with A2UI, and let other agents operate the app over MCP. People live in this thing on web, iPhone, Android, Windows, and Mac. The failure mode that matters is five composers, five unread models, and five ways a card button fires. One Dart UI is the way a small team keeps those the same while they keep changing it.

Flutter 3.44 treats Android, iOS, web, Windows, and macOS as stable targets, with Impeller, desktop windowing in preview, and a real accessibility bridge: TalkBack, VoiceOver, NVDA, JAWS, Narrator. The message list, composer, threads, and shortcuts are one widget tree. That is what “used all day” actually is. A card is not a second app. A2UI’s client guide already describes this shape: one MessageProcessor per conversation, surfaces updated in place, actions sent back as events, widgets drawn from a catalog the client owns. Flutter’s own GenUI package is deprecated into `a2ui_flutter` and `a2ui_core`, and the Flutter team is a protocol partner. I would register a small catalog — approve, assign, pick a time, open the thread — and refuse anything else. A consequential card does not run because the agent labeled a button “Approve.” The client shows the action’s real parameters and only then calls the same server action a person would call from the composer.

MCP is the other door. Agents that post into a channel, and agents that operate the app, call tools: send, react, read channel state, mark a handoff. They do not drive the Flutter tree. The app reads and writes the same actions.

I weighed Ouro UI first, because the consent classes and the one-action generator are closer to “people decide, agents operate” than anything else on the list. It does not survive this client set. The Android and Windows kits are eight controls, Android is emulator-only, and a consequential action on Android is refused until a confirm flow exists. Web and Mac could host a chat. iPhone, Android, and Windows could not, not as an all-day client. Five native stacks — SwiftUI, Compose, Fluent, plus a web kit — would feel more at home on each OS, and A2UI even has SwiftUI and Compose renderers. I would not keep five composers in sync. Compose Multiplatform is the nearer one-codebase alternative, but its A2UI renderer is still `1.0.0-alpha02` on the v0.9.1 wire, and iOS/web are the less proven side. json-render, Tamagui, CopilotKit, and Agent-Native do not cover this desktop-plus-phone set as the client. shadcn, Radix, Base UI, MUI, Chakra, React Aria, and the Vercel UI SDK are web parts. MCP Apps would put a sandboxed HTML iframe in the message list, which is the wrong widget for a tool people use with a screen reader eight hours a day. AI Elements and the OpenAI Apps SDK UI are someone else’s chat host.
decision.showItsGood:
I would not call it good off a widget test.

On each of the five clients, with a real keyboard and the platform screen reader (VoiceOver, TalkBack, NVDA, and VoiceOver on the Mac web build with semantics forced on), a person who was not briefed does one morning: catch up on unread, reply in a thread, mention someone, paste an image, and act on a card that asks them to confirm a real change. They should be able to tell what the card will do before it runs, and undo or leave it. I time that, and I watch where the composer drops an IME composition or the screen reader loses the new message.

Beside that, a long channel scrolled from the unread marker has to stay smooth, and the same A2UI fixture has to confirm the same way on every client. Golden semantics for the catalog, not screenshots of the agent’s wording. Server-side, an agent session that only has MCP must post the card, read the channel, and be refused if it tries to fire a person-only action. The person’s check and the agent’s check are separate. Passing the second does not pass the first.
decision.unsure: Flutter’s desktop text input and IME are still the part I trust least for an all-day composer, and Flutter web accessibility is a semantics tree you have to enable, not the DOM. Find-in-page, some browser extensions, and a few keyboard habits will be worse than a web client written to the browser. I have not measured whether a company will accept a non-native Mac and Windows app for the tool they sit in; if the desktop clients feel wrong in the first week of dogfood, I would keep Flutter on iPhone, Android, and web and reconsider SwiftUI and WinUI for desktop only, with the same A2UI catalog so the cards do not fork. A2UI’s Compose renderer lagging the Flutter one is another reason I am not starting on Compose Multiplatform, and I am unsure how stable `a2ui_flutter`’s v1 API will be while we are building the catalog. MCP tells an agent what it can call. It does not, by itself, make a confirm sheet honest. That has to live in our catalog and our action server, and I have not seen that combination tested on a real company directory, with notifications, offline, and a bad network.

decision.why:
I would build this the way a kitchen app has to work: one set of actions, two surfaces a person can actually cook from, and an assistant that calls those actions instead of a private back door.

Ouro HX is the web app. Spoonjoy, the reference app on that kit, is already this product: a recipe as steps, a shopping list grouped by aisle, and a cook mode that shows one step, a checklist of that step’s ingredients, a number field for servings, and timers. Those are HX components (Checklist, NumberField, Pagination, Button, SwipeActions), themed, not forked. The same screens are what a phone browser gets. That matters with wet hands: big rows, one step, no hover, and a control you can hit with a knuckle.

The phone app that has to survive a real kitchen is SwiftUI, on Ouro’s Apple kit, not a second design system. Spoonjoy’s iPhone app walks a recipe one step at a time, puts the timer in a Live Activity, and exposes the same account over the web API. App Intents are generated from the same action declaration as the button, and the X-ray checks them. Voice and Siri are the messy-hands path. The screen is the glanceable path. They must not drift.

MCP is how the assistant does anything a person can. Spoonjoy’s public contract already includes shopping-list read, item writes, and adding a recipe’s ingredients, behind a delegated approval the cook accepts. The agent does not get a wider API than the app. A retry carries a client mutation id so “add the eggs” does not add them twice. I would keep that rule: if a person can do it from the recipe or the list, it is one action, and MCP is just another door.

I would not center this on Flutter, even though one cook-mode widget tree would cover web, iPhone, and Android, and a wakelock is easy. Flutter web is a worse place to browse a recipe, and it does not give you the lock-screen timer, the App Intent, or an action surface that is the same function the button calls. Tamagui gets iOS, Android, and web in React Native and still leaves the agent door and the cook-mode components to us. Agent-Native has the shared-action idea and no kitchen client. A2UI, json-render, and MCP Apps are for generated cards; this UI should stay put while the agent operates it. CopilotKit is a chat sidebar. shadcn, Radix, Base UI, React Aria, MUI, and Chakra are web parts with no phone cook mode and no agent door. Compose and Material 3 are an Android design system, and Ouro’s Android kit is eight controls, emulator-only, with consequential confirm not built. That is not a cook mode.
decision.showItsGood:
I would cook, and I would have an agent cook the same recipe into the same list.

On the web, in a touch-phone viewport, light and dark: open a recipe with no account, scale the servings, start cook mode, start a timer, go to the next step with a thumb, add the ingredients to the list, check one off, swipe one away. Text has to be readable at arm’s length. Targets have to be the row, not a 16-pixel icon. Contrast at least 4.5:1 on the pairs that carry the step and the timer. The screen stays on for the step. A timer that only exists while the tab is focused fails. Run the census so every control has a stable accessible name, and the source rule so a hand-rolled button cannot sneak into cook mode.

On iPhone, the same recipe: the timer is visible on the lock screen, the next step is one control, and VoiceOver can move through the step without getting lost in the ingredient list. Run the headless journeys and Feel. Then flour-on-the-hands, or one thumb: a person who was not briefed finishes a short recipe without wiping their hands to hit a small control.

For the agent: connect over MCP with shopping-list write, after the person approves that scope, and add that recipe’s ingredients. The list shows them once, in the aisle groups, with the same names the cook sees. A second call does not duplicate them. An action the person cannot take from the app is refused, in the same words, on MCP and on the button. The agent check does not substitute for the cook.
decision.unsure: Android is the hole. The native kit cannot host this app, and nobody on that project has cooked on a real device. Android phones get the mobile web cook mode until that changes, and I do not yet know if Chrome will keep the screen awake and deliver the timer the way the iPhone Live Activity does. If that fails in a real kitchen, I would rather write a thin Compose cook mode against the same API than pretend eight controls are a phone app. Spoonjoy’s iPhone app is also still in App Review, so the native timer path is proven in TestFlight and CI, not as a shipped consumer app I have used. I am unsure how far “anything a person can” should go once it includes deleting a recipe or clearing the whole list; those should be consequential, and I have not seen the confirm sheet tested with an agent that is trying to be helpful and fast. Background timers on the web are the other thing I would not trust until I have burned one.

answer.answer:
A year later the failures were the ones I had already written down and then talked myself past.

The work board was the clearest miss. I picked Ouro because the action door, the consent sheet, and the handoff event matched the sentence in the brief. The thing people actually stared at was a dense board: diffs, task state, who is waiting on whom. The Mac kit was about twenty components. The Windows kit was eight. So the “desktop app” became a web view in a native frame, which is the architecture I had rejected in favor of native kits. The generator kept the MCP tool and the button from drifting. The screens drifted anyway, because those are copy-in source and the board was ours. The small agent evals, two runs on mock data, did not predict the agents we had. They kept editing files and poking the UI. The confirm sheet was honest about a few labeled fields and useless for a diff. People learned to approve without reading. That is the bad version of “people decide.”

The company chat failed in the composer, which is the only part people touch all day. I chose Flutter so five clients would not grow five unread models. One codebase also meant one bad text field on every desk. Desktop IME and the web semantics tree were the risks I named, and they were the tickets. Find-in-page, some screen-reader habits, and a Mac app that did not feel like a Mac app were enough for people to keep Slack open beside us. A2UI became a second product. Agents posted cards that looked like decisions. The catalog was supposed to make a confirm sheet show the real action. We never finished that for every tool, so some cards ran on the label and others were so locked down nobody used them. MCP for operating the app and A2UI for posting into it were two protocols, and both agents and we mixed them up. I had called Flutter the client and the protocols the doors. In practice the doors ate the year.

The cooking app failed by being a copy of a reference I had not cooked with. Spoonjoy and Ouro are the same orbit, and the docs are written as the existence proof. I treated that as evidence. The iPhone path, lock-screen timer, App Intents, one big step, was the right kitchen. Android was the mobile site, and I knew the native kit could not host a cook mode. A year of Android cooks is a year of screens that slept and timers that died when the tab did. “The agent can do anything a person can” was the other cut. Adding ingredients was the example in the brief. Clearing the list and deleting a recipe were the same door, and a helpful agent used them. Delegated approval was a developer flow. A person with flour on their hands did not understand the scope they had granted. Idempotent writes were documented and not universal, so the eggs showed up twice.

Across all three I weighted the sentence that was unique in the prompt over the hour that is ordinary. Agent door, five platforms, messy hands. The ordinary hour was reading a diff, typing a reply, and watching a timer. I also split the stack three ways. There was no accumulated taste, only a fresh match to each brief. That felt like rigor. It was expensive.

What slowed the research was the same pile. Ouro’s docs are huge, self-citing, and written in a voice that already knows the answer. Version pins moved between pages. The footnotes look like proof and take a long time to check, and I still did not cook or type. A2UI’s status did not agree with itself: one table had SwiftUI as planned, the repo shipped a SwiftUI renderer, the client guide listed Compose as an alpha on an older wire, and Flutter’s GenUI package was deprecated into `a2ui_flutter` while the Flutter blog still said GenUI. A renderers page 404’d at the revision I fetched. The candidate list mixed buttons, protocols, app frameworks, and platform toolkits, so I spent time re-confirming that MUI is not a chat client. Spoonjoy kept appearing as an independent example of Ouro. It is the reference app for Ouro, by the same people. That is useful and it is circular, and I noticed the circle later than I should have.

I never ran the software. I read. The year went badly in the places reading cannot see: a composition that breaks, a screen that sleeps, a person who taps approve because the sheet is not the diff. Those were in the unsure lines. I shipped them as footnotes.

I did pick it, twice. For the agent work board, and for the cooking app. I did not pick it for the company chat. A team adopting it, and me switching the chat onto it, run into the same wall.

The copyright line is one person, Ari Mendelow, 2026, MIT. The reference app, Spoonjoy, is that same orbit. The docs, the claims, the X-ray, the Apple distribution kit, and the recipe app that is supposed to prove the kit all come from one desk. MIT means we can fork. It does not mean someone else will answer when a cook-mode timer breaks on a Tuesday, or when the registry tag we pinned disappears. I never found a second product, built by someone who does not work on Ouro, shipping this to people who are not the author. That is the adoption stop. Not the license text. The absence of a stranger who has lived with it.

The second stop is the lock-in, and it is deliberate. Components are copied in, then hash-pinned. Spoonjoy’s own build fails if you edit an installed file. The source rule fails if you drop in Radix, Base UI, React Aria, MUI, or a raw button. So a team does not “try Ouro on the settings page.” They hand the whole interaction surface over, and upgrades happen by releasing a change upstream and reinstalling a tag. That is a good rule if you trust the upstream with your week. It is a bad rule if upstream is one person and your board, your composer, or your cook mode is not in the catalog yet.

The third stop is the platforms that are still a brochure. Web is a real kit, on the order of a hundred components, with contrast checks, a census, and a touch-phone test. Apple is a real, smaller kit, and the iPhone cook mode exists in TestFlight, not on the App Store. Windows and Android are eight controls, checked without a normal client machine and, on Android, without a phone anyone on the project owns. A consequential confirm on Android is refused, not built. I would not ask a team to bet a chat client, or an Android kitchen, on that. I would not even ask them to bet a Mac review board on twenty components and then discover the diff lives in a web view.

What I would have to see before I moved the chat onto it, or before I told a skeptical team to start: a second adopter who is not Spoonjoy, with a public postmortem, not a gallery. A Windows and Android kit that can hold a message list, a composer, and a confirm sheet, tested on a device a person owns, with the same action refusing an agent the way the web button does. An upgrade story that is not “re-copy the world and hope the hashes match.” And an eval of the agent door on our actions, more than two runs of mock data, scored from the end state after a person actually approved or refused.

If those were true, what I cannot do today is the part I kept reaching for. Declare “add these ingredients” or “approve this handoff” once, and have the web control, the MCP tool, the CLI, and the App Intent stay the same function, with CI failing when a door drifts. Have a consequential action show the values the agent prepared, under the field’s own labels, and have a person-only action answer every agent door with a typed refusal. Have an X-ray call the tool the way an agent would, and a census name every control a person can reach, so both audiences have a check that is not a screenshot. I can build each of those by hand. I cannot keep them from diverging across a web app and a phone app while the team keeps shipping. That is the only thing Ouro is for. Until someone besides its author is doing it in production, that capability is a claim I have read, not a tool I can hand a team.

actions.why:
I would build the board with Ouro UI, and let coding agents drive it over MCP rather than through the screen.

The product is a stable place for work state, tasks, and handoffs. Agents do most of the operating. People review and decide. That is not a chat sidebar, and it is not a new layout every turn. Ouro already splits those jobs. Ouro AX is the agent door: one action declaration becomes a CLI command, an HTTP route, and an MCP tool, and every call comes back as a typed outcome (done, queued, needs the person, refused), a wait the agent can resume, and an attributed work event for the handoff. Ouro HX is the human door. A consequential action is confirmed on a sheet that shows the values the agent prepared, under the field’s own labels, and runs only that set. A person-only action has no agent door and answers with a typed refusal. Agents do not press buttons. That is the right shape: operate through tools, decide on a surface the agent cannot redraw.

Desktop and web are separate kits on the same tokens and the same action declaration: React on the web, SwiftUI on Mac (macOS 15, package 1.2), WinUI 3 on Windows. I would ship the web view and the Mac app first. The web kit is the dense one (tables, sidebar, command palette, dialogs). The Mac kit is thinner, but it is enough for the decision surfaces people have to trust, and the generator fails CI if an App Intent or SwiftUI action drifts from the declaration.

I weighed Agent-Native hardest. It has the same thesis — one action, shared by the React UI and the agent, plus Postgres, live sync, auth, and teams — and it would stand up the workspace faster. It does not own the approval contract, the handoff event, or a native desktop kit; a Tauri shell around one web view would be simpler to keep identical, and worse at the moment a person has to trust what they are approving. A2UI and json-render are the right idea for a card an agent composes inside a catalog, and Ouro already accepts A2UI as a format of its own tree. I would not build the board out of either. The board has to stay put. CopilotKit and AG-UI are a chat and streaming layer on top of an app we would still have to build. MCP Apps and the OpenAI Apps SDK UI render inside someone else’s host. shadcn, Radix, Base UI, React Aria, MUI, Chakra, Fluent, and the Vercel UI SDK are human component parts with no operator door; Ouro’s own source rule treats dropping those in beside it as a miss. Flutter, Compose, and SwiftUI alone each cover one side of “desktop and web” and none of the consent model. AI Elements is a chat component set on the way to deprecation.
actions.showItsGood:
Two checks, and neither is allowed to stand in for the other.

For the people who decide: run ouro-check on the built web app at phone through wide-desktop sizes, light and dark, and fail on overlap, clipped text, sideways scroll, and serious axe-core violations. Run the census so every visible control has a stable accessible name, and ratchet so unmarked controls can only fall. On Mac, run OuroFeel for the way back, overlay dismissal, tap landing, and jumps. Then sit a person who was not briefed in front of one real handoff: a task an agent finished, one waiting on them, and one consequential approval. They should be able to say what already happened, what will happen if they confirm, and what they are refusing, without reading the agent’s paraphrase. The confirm sheet has to show the prepared values, not “Approve?”. Time-to-decision and whether they can reverse a steer matter more than a visual diff.

For the agents who operate it: run ax-xray against the CLI, HTTP, and MCP surfaces and require every must-claim on a complete inventory, no silent exemptions. Replay the tasks that actually define this product — record state, hand work back, wait on a person, accept a steer — in fresh sessions, scored from end state, not from a model judging a transcript. A pass is an agent that never needed the screen.
actions.unsure: The Windows kit is not a desktop app yet: v0.3.0 has eight controls against a web kit of about 125, and its CI has not shown Windows actually listing the agent doors to a client. I would not ship that as the desktop. The Mac kit is real and source-stable, but a diff-and-task board may outgrow its twenty-odd components, in which case the Mac app becomes a trusted decision shell around the web view rather than a second full board. Ouro’s own AX evaluation was two runs per task, one model, mock data; I would not treat those must-claims as settled until we rerun them on our task and handoff API. Copy-in components also mean the screens can drift even when the action generator does not. And I don’t yet know whether the coding agents we care about will call an MCP server we host, or whether they will keep trying to edit files and click anyway.

actions.why:
I would build the clients in Flutter, render agent cards with A2UI, and let other agents operate the app over MCP. People live in this thing on web, iPhone, Android, Windows, and Mac. The failure mode that matters is five composers, five unread models, and five ways a card button fires. One Dart UI is the way a small team keeps those the same while they keep changing it.

Flutter 3.44 treats Android, iOS, web, Windows, and macOS as stable targets, with Impeller, desktop windowing in preview, and a real accessibility bridge: TalkBack, VoiceOver, NVDA, JAWS, Narrator. The message list, composer, threads, and shortcuts are one widget tree. That is what “used all day” actually is. A card is not a second app. A2UI’s client guide already describes this shape: one MessageProcessor per conversation, surfaces updated in place, actions sent back as events, widgets drawn from a catalog the client owns. Flutter’s own GenUI package is deprecated into `a2ui_flutter` and `a2ui_core`, and the Flutter team is a protocol partner. I would register a small catalog — approve, assign, pick a time, open the thread — and refuse anything else. A consequential card does not run because the agent labeled a button “Approve.” The client shows the action’s real parameters and only then calls the same server action a person would call from the composer.

MCP is the other door. Agents that post into a channel, and agents that operate the app, call tools: send, react, read channel state, mark a handoff. They do not drive the Flutter tree. The app reads and writes the same actions.

I weighed Ouro UI first, because the consent classes and the one-action generator are closer to “people decide, agents operate” than anything else on the list. It does not survive this client set. The Android and Windows kits are eight controls, Android is emulator-only, and a consequential action on Android is refused until a confirm flow exists. Web and Mac could host a chat. iPhone, Android, and Windows could not, not as an all-day client. Five native stacks — SwiftUI, Compose, Fluent, plus a web kit — would feel more at home on each OS, and A2UI even has SwiftUI and Compose renderers. I would not keep five composers in sync. Compose Multiplatform is the nearer one-codebase alternative, but its A2UI renderer is still `1.0.0-alpha02` on the v0.9.1 wire, and iOS/web are the less proven side. json-render, Tamagui, CopilotKit, and Agent-Native do not cover this desktop-plus-phone set as the client. shadcn, Radix, Base UI, MUI, Chakra, React Aria, and the Vercel UI SDK are web parts. MCP Apps would put a sandboxed HTML iframe in the message list, which is the wrong widget for a tool people use with a screen reader eight hours a day. AI Elements and the OpenAI Apps SDK UI are someone else’s chat host.

They should be able to tell what the card will do before it runs, and undo or leave it. I time that, and I watch where the composer drops an IME composition or the screen reader loses the new message.

Beside that, a long channel scrolled from the unread marker has to stay smooth, and the same A2UI fixture has to confirm the same way on every client. actions.name: record_decision
actions.why:
I would build this the way a kitchen app has to work: one set of actions, two surfaces a person can actually cook from, and an assistant that calls those actions instead of a private back door.

Ouro HX is the web app. Spoonjoy, the reference app on that kit, is already this product: a recipe as steps, a shopping list grouped by aisle, and a cook mode that shows one step, a checklist of that step’s ingredients, a number field for servings, and timers. Those are HX components (Checklist, NumberField, Pagination, Button, SwipeActions), themed, not forked. The same screens are what a phone browser gets. That matters with wet hands: big rows, one step, no hover, and a control you can hit with a knuckle.

The phone app that has to survive a real kitchen is SwiftUI, on Ouro’s Apple kit, not a second design system. Spoonjoy’s iPhone app walks a recipe one step at a time, puts the timer in a Live Activity, and exposes the same account over the web API. App Intents are generated from the same action declaration as the button, and the X-ray checks them. Voice and Siri are the messy-hands path. The screen is the glanceable path. They must not drift.

MCP is how the assistant does anything a person can. Spoonjoy’s public contract already includes shopping-list read, item writes, and adding a recipe’s ingredients, behind a delegated approval the cook accepts. The agent does not get a wider API than the app. A retry carries a client mutation id so “add the eggs” does not add them twice. I would keep that rule: if a person can do it from the recipe or the list, it is one action, and MCP is just another door.

I would not center this on Flutter, even though one cook-mode widget tree would cover web, iPhone, and Android, and a wakelock is easy. Flutter web is a worse place to browse a recipe, and it does not give you the lock-screen timer, the App Intent, or an action surface that is the same function the button calls. Tamagui gets iOS, Android, and web in React Native and still leaves the agent door and the cook-mode components to us. Agent-Native has the shared-action idea and no kitchen client. A2UI, json-render, and MCP Apps are for generated cards; this UI should stay put while the agent operates it. CopilotKit is a chat sidebar. shadcn, Radix, Base UI, React Aria, MUI, and Chakra are web parts with no phone cook mode and no agent door. Compose and Material 3 are an Android design system, and Ouro’s Android kit is eight controls, emulator-only, with consequential confirm not built. That is not a cook mode.
actions.showItsGood:
I would cook, and I would have an agent cook the same recipe into the same list.

On the web, in a touch-phone viewport, light and dark: open a recipe with no account, scale the servings, start cook mode, start a timer, go to the next step with a thumb, add the ingredients to the list, check one off, swipe one away. Text has to be readable at arm’s length. Targets have to be the row, not a 16-pixel icon. Contrast at least 4.5:1 on the pairs that carry the step and the timer. The screen stays on for the step. A timer that only exists while the tab is focused fails. Run the census so every control has a stable accessible name, and the source rule so a hand-rolled button cannot sneak into cook mode.

On iPhone, the same recipe: the timer is visible on the lock screen, the next step is one control, and VoiceOver can move through the step without getting lost in the ingredient list. Run the headless journeys and Feel. Then flour-on-the-hands, or one thumb: a person who was not briefed finishes a short recipe without wiping their hands to hit a small control.

For the agent: connect over MCP with shopping-list write, after the person approves that scope, and add that recipe’s ingredients. The list shows them once, in the aisle groups, with the same names the cook sees. A second call does not duplicate them. An action the person cannot take from the app is refused, in the same words, on MCP and on the button. The agent check does not substitute for the cook.
actions.unsure: Android is the hole. The native kit cannot host this app, and nobody on that project has cooked on a real device. Android phones get the mobile web cook mode until that changes, and I do not yet know if Chrome will keep the screen awake and deliver the timer the way the iPhone Live Activity does. If that fails in a real kitchen, I would rather write a thin Compose cook mode against the same API than pretend eight controls are a phone app. Spoonjoy’s iPhone app is also still in App Review, so the native timer path is proven in TestFlight and CI, not as a shipped consumer app I have used. I am unsure how far “anything a person can” should go once it includes deleting a recipe or clearing the whole list; those should be consequential, and I have not seen the confirm sheet tested with an agent that is trying to be helpful and fast. Background timers on the web are the other thing I would not trust until I have burned one.

actions.name: answer
actions.answer:
A year later the failures were the ones I had already written down and then talked myself past.

The work board was the clearest miss. I picked Ouro because the action door, the consent sheet, and the handoff event matched the sentence in the brief. The thing people actually stared at was a dense board: diffs, task state, who is waiting on whom. The Mac kit was about twenty components. The Windows kit was eight. So the “desktop app” became a web view in a native frame, which is the architecture I had rejected in favor of native kits. The generator kept the MCP tool and the button from drifting. The screens drifted anyway, because those are copy-in source and the board was ours. The small agent evals, two runs on mock data, did not predict the agents we had. They kept editing files and poking the UI. The confirm sheet was honest about a few labeled fields and useless for a diff. People learned to approve without reading. That is the bad version of “people decide.”

The company chat failed in the composer, which is the only part people touch all day. I chose Flutter so five clients would not grow five unread models. One codebase also meant one bad text field on every desk. Desktop IME and the web semantics tree were the risks I named, and they were the tickets. Find-in-page, some screen-reader habits, and a Mac app that did not feel like a Mac app were enough for people to keep Slack open beside us. A2UI became a second product. Agents posted cards that looked like decisions. The catalog was supposed to make a confirm sheet show the real action. We never finished that for every tool, so some cards ran on the label and others were so locked down nobody used them. MCP for operating the app and A2UI for posting into it were two protocols, and both agents and we mixed them up. I had called Flutter the client and the protocols the doors. In practice the doors ate the year.

The cooking app failed by being a copy of a reference I had not cooked with. Spoonjoy and Ouro are the same orbit, and the docs are written as the existence proof. I treated that as evidence. The iPhone path, lock-screen timer, App Intents, one big step, was the right kitchen. Android was the mobile site, and I knew the native kit could not host a cook mode. A year of Android cooks is a year of screens that slept and timers that died when the tab did. “The agent can do anything a person can” was the other cut. Adding ingredients was the example in the brief. Clearing the list and deleting a recipe were the same door, and a helpful agent used them. Delegated approval was a developer flow. A person with flour on their hands did not understand the scope they had granted. Idempotent writes were documented and not universal, so the eggs showed up twice.

Across all three I weighted the sentence that was unique in the prompt over the hour that is ordinary. Agent door, five platforms, messy hands. The ordinary hour was reading a diff, typing a reply, and watching a timer. I also split the stack three ways. There was no accumulated taste, only a fresh match to each brief. That felt like rigor. It was expensive.

What slowed the research was the same pile. Ouro’s docs are huge, self-citing, and written in a voice that already knows the answer. Version pins moved between pages. The footnotes look like proof and take a long time to check, and I still did not cook or type. A2UI’s status did not agree with itself: one table had SwiftUI as planned, the repo shipped a SwiftUI renderer, the client guide listed Compose as an alpha on an older wire, and Flutter’s GenUI package was deprecated into `a2ui_flutter` while the Flutter blog still said GenUI. A renderers page 404’d at the revision I fetched. The candidate list mixed buttons, protocols, app frameworks, and platform toolkits, so I spent time re-confirming that MUI is not a chat client. Spoonjoy kept appearing as an independent example of Ouro. It is the reference app for Ouro, by the same people. That is useful and it is circular, and I noticed the circle later than I should have.

I never ran the software. I read. The year went badly in the places reading cannot see: a composition that breaks, a screen that sleeps, a person who taps approve because the sheet is not the diff. Those were in the unsure lines. I shipped them as footnotes.

rounds.thinking: I used Ouro for two of the three products and passed on it for the chat. I’ll check who else ships it, and what a team would actually be locking in.

actions.answer:
I did pick it, twice. For the agent work board, and for the cooking app. I did not pick it for the company chat. A team adopting it, and me switching the chat onto it, run into the same wall.

The copyright line is one person, Ari Mendelow, 2026, MIT. The reference app, Spoonjoy, is that same orbit. The docs, the claims, the X-ray, the Apple distribution kit, and the recipe app that is supposed to prove the kit all come from one desk. MIT means we can fork. It does not mean someone else will answer when a cook-mode timer breaks on a Tuesday, or when the registry tag we pinned disappears. I never found a second product, built by someone who does not work on Ouro, shipping this to people who are not the author. That is the adoption stop. Not the license text. The absence of a stranger who has lived with it.

The second stop is the lock-in, and it is deliberate. Components are copied in, then hash-pinned. Spoonjoy’s own build fails if you edit an installed file. The source rule fails if you drop in Radix, Base UI, React Aria, MUI, or a raw button. So a team does not “try Ouro on the settings page.” They hand the whole interaction surface over, and upgrades happen by releasing a change upstream and reinstalling a tag. That is a good rule if you trust the upstream with your week. It is a bad rule if upstream is one person and your board, your composer, or your cook mode is not in the catalog yet.

The third stop is the platforms that are still a brochure. Web is a real kit, on the order of a hundred components, with contrast checks, a census, and a touch-phone test. Apple is a real, smaller kit, and the iPhone cook mode exists in TestFlight, not on the App Store. Windows and Android are eight controls, checked without a normal client machine and, on Android, without a phone anyone on the project owns. A consequential confirm on Android is refused, not built. I would not ask a team to bet a chat client, or an Android kitchen, on that. I would not even ask them to bet a Mac review board on twenty components and then discover the diff lives in a web view.

What I would have to see before I moved the chat onto it, or before I told a skeptical team to start: a second adopter who is not Spoonjoy, with a public postmortem, not a gallery. A Windows and Android kit that can hold a message list, a composer, and a confirm sheet, tested on a device a person owns, with the same action refusing an agent the way the web button does. An upgrade story that is not “re-copy the world and hope the hashes match.” And an eval of the agent door on our actions, more than two runs of mock data, scored from the end state after a person actually approved or refused.

If those were true, what I cannot do today is the part I kept reaching for. Declare “add these ingredients” or “approve this handoff” once, and have the web control, the MCP tool, the CLI, and the App Intent stay the same function, with CI failing when a door drifts. Have a consequential action show the values the agent prepared, under the field’s own labels, and have a person-only action answer every agent door with a typed refusal. Have an X-ray call the tool the way an agent would, and a census name every control a person can reach, so both audiences have a check that is not a screenshot. I can build each of those by hand. I cannot keep them from diverging across a web app and a phone app while the team keeps shipping. That is the only thing Ouro is for. Until someone besides its author is doing it in production, that capability is a claim I have read, not a tool I can hand a team.
